learningObjective: Reason about the trade-off between torch.compile's compile-time cost and steady-state kernel performance.

canonicalClaims.claim: torch.compile has a non-trivial compile-time cost (tracing, AOTAutograd, Inductor codegen, and — under max-autotune — kernel search) that must be amortized across enough steps to yield a net speedup over eager; short-running scripts may not amortize the cost, while long-running loops usually do.
conditions: Measurements include the first-call compile time.
nonImplications: Does not imply torch.compile is universally slower for short runs; warm caches change the picture.
Does not imply autotune search space is constant across releases.

misconceptions.claim: torch.compile adds per-call runtime overhead of seconds.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Steady-state per-call overhead is small; the seconds come from initial compile.

misconceptions.claim: max-autotune sacrifices numerical accuracy for speed.
misconceptions.whyWrong: It explores configs but preserves numerical semantics.

misconceptions.claim: GIL contention is the reason short torch.compile runs are slower.
misconceptions.whyWrong: GIL is unrelated to this specific compile-time cost effect.

misconceptions.claim: Compile time can be ignored when comparing eager vs. compile for a run.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Ignoring compile time inflates the perceived speedup; honest benchmarks include it.

implementationFacts: First-call compile includes tracing + AOTAutograd + Inductor codegen + autotune search (under max-autotune)
Subsequent calls hit the compile cache (in-memory by default)
Warm-up runs are standard when benchmarking compiled code
performanceScenarios: Choosing when torch.compile is worth it requires comparing amortized runtime including compile time.
